hook: The church official who moved the Earth out of the centre of the universe.

pages.x: Nicolaus Copernicus was born in 1473 in Toruń, in Poland. When his father died, his uncle, a bishop, paid for him to study in Kraków and then in Italy, at Bologna, Padua and Ferrara, where he studied law, medicine and astronomy.

He spent most of his life as a canon, a church official, at Frombork cathedral on the Baltic coast. He ran estates, worked as a doctor, and wrote about money, noticing that bad coins drive good ones out of use. At night he watched the sky from a tower.
For 1,400 years astronomers taught that the Earth stood still at the centre and everything circled it. Copernicus showed the planets made more sense if the Earth and the planets circle the Sun.
pages.fx: It moved the Earth from the centre of the universe. Galileo, Kepler and Newton built on it, and the scientific revolution began.

pages.x: He wrote a short sketch of his idea around 1514, but held back the full book for nearly 30 years, afraid of being laughed at. A young mathematician, Rheticus, came to stay with him in 1539 and finally talked him into it.

On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was printed in 1543. A story says the first copy was put into his hands on the day he died. Its editor slipped in an unsigned preface saying it was only a way of calculating, not the truth.

His grave was lost for centuries. In 2005 archaeologists found a skeleton under the floor of Frombork cathedral, and in 2008 hairs found in one of his old books matched its DNA. He was reburied with honours in 2010.
Copernicus started the scientific revolution. A "Copernican revolution" now means any idea that turns the old picture of the world upside down.
pts: Put the Sun at the centre of the planets
